title: Tree indexing: ISAM and B+ trees
lead: Leaves store data entries. Internal nodes use separator keys to choose a search branch. The same value can appear in both places with different roles.
goals: Use separators to find a leaf and scan a range
Simulate insertion and deletion using the order-d convention
Explain copy-up, push-up, and byte-based occupancy

sections.title: The conceptual framework
sections.html:
ISAM keeps its internal-node structure fixed. When a leaf runs out of space, it adds an overflow page to hold extra entries. A B+ tree balances dynamically: all leaves are at the same depth, links connect leaves for ordered scans, and updates may split nodes, redistribute entries, or merge nodes.

Fanout is the number of children of a node. Under this lesson’s order-d convention, a non-root leaf contains d to 2d data entries. A non-root internal node contains d to 2d separator keys. It has one more child pointer than separator keys, giving d+1 to 2d+1 children. A separator is a boundary value used to choose a search branch. The root has exceptions to the minimum occupancy rule. The lesson also considers fanout, caching upper levels, practical deletion policies, occupancy with variable-length entries, prefix compression, and suffix truncation.

Textbook occupancy and production policies

The textbook non-root occupancy rule does not describe every production deletion policy. Some implementations leave underfull nodes and reclaim them only when empty, reducing immediate maintenance. Variable-length keys or RID lists make fullness a byte-capacity question rather than just an entry count. Internal and leaf entries can have different sizes. In the simple count model, an internal root has at least two children unless its only child is replacing it; an empty tree can be represented by a root leaf.

Original supplementary explanation and practice. Sources: Lecture 9 · physical PDF pp. 13, 14, 16, 26, 27, 28, 29.

sections.title: An original insertion: copying a leaf key upwards
sections.html:
Choose d=2, so each leaf holds at most 2d=4 entries. The root is currently the leaf [4,9,12,18]. Inserting 15 in order produces [4,9,12,15,18]. Its five entries exceed the leaf’s capacity.

  1. Split it into a left leaf [4,9] and a right leaf [12,15,18]. They contain two and three entries respectively, both within the permitted range from d=2 to 2d=4.
  2. Create a new root with separator [12] and pointers to the two leaves. Keys <12 go left; keys ≥12 go right.
  3. Keep 12 in the right leaf. The copy of 12 in the root only selects the search branch. This operation is called copy-up.
  4. Connect the leaves with next/prev links so an ordered scan can move between them.

Searching for 15 follows the ≥12 branch and finds 15 in the right leaf. Searching for 10 follows the <12 branch and finds no matching entry. To scan the inclusive range 8..16, start in the left leaf, retain 9, then follow its link to collect 12 and 15 from the right leaf. The result is [9,12,15].

Key takeaway

Copy-up retains the data key in the leaf. The root’s copy of 12 is used for routing. The leaf must retain 12 so that a scan through the leaves reads all the data entries.

A separate internal-node split with new data. An internal node temporarily contains keys [10,20,30,40,50] and six children. Push the middle separator, 30, up into the parent. The resulting internal nodes contain [10,20] and [40,50], with three children each. Unlike a leaf split, 30 no longer appears as a separator in either of those two nodes. Push-up moves a separator; it does not delete a data entry from a leaf.

sections.title: An original deletion: redistribute, then merge
sections.html:
Start with the tree produced by the leaf split. Delete 4: the left leaf becomes [9], with only one entry, below the minimum d=2. The right leaf [12,15,18] has three entries, so it can lend one while retaining the required two. Move 12 to the left, producing [9,12] and [15,18]. Change the root separator from 12 to 15, the smallest key in the right leaf under this example’s convention.

Key takeaway

Redistributing a key also requires updating the parent’s separator. If the root still stores 12, a search for 12 goes right even though the record has moved left. Valid leaf occupancy alone does not guarantee correct lookup.

Now delete 9. The left leaf contains [12], while the right leaf has exactly two entries and cannot lend one without falling below its minimum. Merge the leaves into [12,15,18], which fits within the four-entry capacity. The root now has no separator and only one child, so replace the root with that leaf. The tree becomes one level shorter.

After each step, check the invariants: in this unique-key example, every data entry occurs exactly once in the leaves; all leaves have the same depth; separators divide key ranges correctly; and occupancy is valid apart from the root’s permitted exception. A tree that merely looks balanced may still route a lookup incorrectly.

Repair internal nodes, not just leaves

Leaf repair and internal-node repair do not move separators in the same way. A leaf merge combines data entries and removes their parent separator; that separator is not inserted as an extra data record. An internal merge pulls the parent separator down between the two key lists and combines their child pointers in order.

For an order-d tree with d=2, let the parent separator be 30, with left internal keys [10,20] and an underfull right node [40]. The nodes have three and two children. Their merge produces [10,20,30,40] with five children. Omitting 30 leaves no separator between the former left and right child ranges. The parent loses one separator and one child pointer, so repair may continue upward. If a root is left with only one child, that child becomes the root.

For redistribution, let the parent separator be 40, the left internal sibling [10,20,30], and the underfull right sibling [60]. Move the left sibling’s rightmost child to the right sibling’s leftmost position. Move 40 down into the right node and 30 up to the parent. The result is left [10,20], parent [30], right [40,60]. Moving a separator without its associated child pointer breaks routing.

A sibling for these textbook repairs must be adjacent and share the same parent. A neighbouring leaf in the linked leaf chain can have another parent, so leaf adjacency alone does not justify this repair. During insertion, redistributing into a sibling with spare capacity can avoid a split, but requires separator updates and additional I/O.

Original supplementary explanation and practice. Sources: Lecture 9 · physical PDF pp. 17, 18, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25.

sections.title: ISAM, byte capacity, and an open exercise
sections.html:
An original example. An ISAM leaf for the range [20,40) is full. Inserting 27,28,29 may create an overflow chain while leaving the root unchanged. Under the same workload, a B+ tree may change its structure through splitting. Its maintenance costs differ, but adding data does not necessarily increase its height.

With variable-length string keys, three long entries may fill a page that could hold ten short entries. In a byte-based simulation, set capacity=256 bytes and include key bytes, pointers, and the header. Do not automatically equate half of the entry count with half of the byte capacity. This is a modelling exercise, not a policy shared by every database engine.

With fanout=100 and 1,000,000 leaf pages, how many edges connect the root to a leaf in an ideal full tree?

log₁₀₀(1,000,000)=3 edges, giving 4 levels when both the root and the leaves are counted. Actual page I/O also depends on which levels are cached and what the leaf entries contain.

ISAM boundaries, prefix compression, and duplicates

ISAM’s fixed internal levels route keys to primary leaf ranges, while overflow chains absorb growth. An internal separator can remain a correct boundary after the leaf entry equal to it is deleted. Primary leaves are allocated in sequence in the lecture’s model; overflow entries need not be sorted. Heavy updates can create long chain scans without deepening the upper tree.

Prefix compression stores a shared beginning once. For cat01, cat02, and cat09, storing prefix cat0 and suffixes 1, 2, and 9 preserves the full keys. Suffix truncation of an internal separator has a different aim: retain enough information to route searches correctly. Under ordinary lexicographic order, a boundary between left keys beginning apple and right keys beginning banana can use b if every left key is below b and every right key is at least b. That separator need not be a complete stored data value. Leaf values must remain recoverable; arbitrarily shortening each leaf key to one character is not lossless.

Duplicate search keys require a design that distinguishes individual entries or stores their RID list. The worked update traces deliberately use unique keys. Equality over duplicates must return every matching entry, even when matches occupy multiple leaves.

Original supplementary explanation and practice. Sources: Lecture 9 · physical PDF pp. 6, 7, 10, 11, 13, 14, 16, 26, 27, 28, 29.

quiz.question: When the leaf [4,9,12,15,18] splits into [4,9] and [12,15,18], what happens to separator 12?
options: It is removed from every leaf
It is copied into the parent and retained in the right leaf
It is retained only in the left leaf
quiz.explanation: Leaves store data entries. The parent’s copy is used for routing, so copy-up retains the original entry in the leaf.
